The world is now in the grip of a super El Niño : a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.
The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we plan for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.
This year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter , sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.
“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” says Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”
El Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.
Both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.
Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains , says Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”
And the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked , and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched . The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.
As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees Celsius—breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees Celsius—and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he says. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.
Unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested —though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.
All these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” says Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer ; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed . Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.
While any year brings its own spates of bad weather —some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change—plenty of events this year have been attributed to El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.
In Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall . In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.
Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second-largest annual crop on record.

Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument
The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.
The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.
Despite mounting pressure, an agreement to discuss an instrument to regulate autonomous weapons over the next two years fell short of the urgent action rights groups said was needed to address the looming threat.
“We’re starting to see artificial intelligence … being fielded in the battlefield and perhaps also already in weapon systems. If we leave this unregulated, it will be much more difficult to put the genie back in the bottle,” said Dr Cordula Droege, the director of international law, movement and partnerships at the ICRC.
Autonomous weapons are military systems that act without human supervision, often through the use of artificial intelligence or other forms of robotics.
As artificial intelligence has grown exponentially in recent years, militaries and manufacturers have created increasingly advanced weapons systems for both offensive and defensive purposes.
These systems include the use of AI in generating target banks , as was done by the Israeli military in Gaza, as well as semi-autonomous drones in the Ukraine-Russia war, which have “last-mile capability”, where AI takes over in the drone’s final approach to its target.
The president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres, have called for a legally binding instrument with clear prohibitions and restrictions on use of weapons. In particular, the ICRC has called for a ban on the use of autonomous weapons against personnel, as well as ensuring that weapons systems behave predictably and placing limits on weapons including restricting their use to military objectives.
Experts have said that given the rapid development of autonomous weapons and AI, the failure to create adequate regulations could have dangerous repercussions.
“It’s not about banning all autonomous weapon systems, but to set limits in an international treaty of red lines that should never be crossed,” said Droege. “We’re very close to crossing those red lines, particularly targeting human beings through machines should be a moral red line.”
Other rights groups warned that any delay towards regulation of these weapons risked allowing private industry and militaries to set the norms of how autonomous weapons are used.
Already, autonomous weapons have led to civilian harm. Three civilians were killed by a Russian drone guided by an AI system in July in Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine. The drone tried to hit a petrol station, probably its intended target, but instead crashed into a wall, killing three people in a fountain of shrapnel.
In Gaza, Israel has used AI-assisted targeting methods to fill its target banks much faster than humanly possible since the start of the war. As a result, rights groups have said that civilians and people with tenuous links to militant groups were erroneously killed.
In Iran, a US strike that hit an elementary school, killing 156 civilians including 120 schoolchildren, reportedly was a result of faulty intelligence gathered by AI systems.
Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said further delay to a strong treaty could see “more cases of mass civilian harm that we’ve seen over the past 18 months to two years”, warning that some of these mass casualty events could dwarf what has already occurred. She said manufacturers and militaries were trying to develop “swarm” capabilities, where hundreds or thousands of autonomous drones act at the same time.
“This has the potential for high damage, just because of the sheer mass of systems that would be autonomous. All it takes is for one of them to face algorithmic error and then the entire swarm is utilised and led down a path based on that error … particularly if they’re programmed to target humans.”
There is also a risk of proliferation, as non-state groups increasingly use AI to program their weapons systems, as was the case when the Houthi movement in Yemen used Claude to “vibe code” ballistic missiles.
Armed Islamist groups in Africa’s Sahel region have reportedly used AI tools to improve drone ballistics and for operational planning.
“This is the only thing that is important this week. It’s not really the substance of laws. What’s on the agenda here, after 13 years, is the political will finally present to start to get serious about regulation of autonomous weapons systems,” said a senior diplomat with knowledge of the UN discussions.

At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones
A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.
Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.
Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.
The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.
“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.
Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.
Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.
“When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.
The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

At least 15 people rescued, including 4 taken to hospital, as authorities say cause of the fire is under investigation.
A fire at a sweets factory in Indonesia has killed at least three people and 36 others are missing.
Photos and videos circulating online on Sunday showed flames and thick smoke coming from the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province, which borders the capital Jakarta. Footage from inside the three-storey building appeared to show the fire caused extensive damage, with equipment blackened and destroyed.
A company representative said 300 workers were inside when the blaze started. He added that 54 were initially missing, but 15 have since been rescued. Four of them were taken to hospital, said the National Search and Rescue Agency in a statement.
“The fire is still burning in several locations and firefighting teams are continuing extinguishing and cooling operations,” rescue official Rizky Dwianto told The Associated Press news agency.
Firefighters from Serang district and Banten province were battling flames in several parts of the facility more than 12 hours after the fire began, Dwianto said.
Rescue workers along with fire department personnel and the Indonesian Red Cross searched different sections of the factory, focusing on areas where victims might be trapped, he added.
The disaster agency said the cause of the fire was under investigation.
Local broadcasters and social media accounts shared footage of families gathering outside the factory.
The factory produces milk-based snacks and sweets, known as Milkita.
Indonesia has suffered a number of deadly fires in recent years. A fire in an office building in Jakarta killed at least 22 people last December. An explosion at an Indonesian nickel-processing plant killed at least 13 people in 2023.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters before drifting into Finnish territory.
A fire on board a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones off the coast of Finland in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, the Finnish coastguard said.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.
Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.
Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois said afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.
“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”
Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.
“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.
Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.
The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.

The result means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, can eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in Game 2 of the best-of-three series in Ohio next Friday.
“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Miami coach Kily González said afterwards.
“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out.
“There’s no better challenge for us as a team than this. It’s a test of character, and I know my team has that character.”
Joaquín Valiente scored twice in the space of two minutes as FC Dallas beat the Portland Timbers 3-0 in the opening game of their best-of-three Western Conference first-round series.
The 25-year-old Uruguayan midfielder broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, volleying home a rebound after Daniel Job’s shot was parried by Portland goalkeeper James Pantemis.
Valiente doubled the lead two minutes later, timing his run to meet another pass from Job before redirecting the ball between Pantemis’s legs.
Samuel Sarver completed the scoring in the fourth minute of stoppage time, finishing a cross from Logan Farrington on the counterattack.
Dallas goalkeeper Daniel de Sousa Britto, known simply as Daniel, made four saves, while Pantemis finished with five for Portland.
The Timbers also lost Ariel Lassiter to an apparent injury in the 33rd minute.
Second-seeded Dallas can advance to the Western Conference semi-finals with a victory in Portland next Saturday.
Teenager Peyton Miller scored one goal and helped create another as the New England Revolution beat the Philadelphia Union 2-0 in the opening game of their Eastern Conference first-round series.
The 19-year-old Miller became the fifth-youngest goalscorer in MLS Cup playoffs history when he volleyed home a cross from Jack Harrison in the 73rd minute, his effort bouncing off the crossbar and into the net.
New England had taken the lead in the 10th minute when Miller’s shot from the edge of the penalty area deflected off Philadelphia defender Nathan Harriel for an own goal.
Harrison, who came on as a substitute in the 62nd minute, was making his first appearance since 9 September after missing more than two months with a quadriceps injury.
Philadelphia nearly equalized in the 37th minute when Cavan Sullivan turned and fired a shot from outside the penalty area that struck the left post.
The Union fielded the youngest starting lineup in MLS Cup playoffs history, with an average age of 23 years and 207 days, breaking the record set by the New York Red Bulls in 2022.
Matt Turner made two saves to preserve the shutout for New England, who can advance to the Eastern Conference semi-finals with a victory in Philadelphia next Saturday.

Lionel Messi escapes a red-card booking for a controversial throw-in in Miami’s 3-0 defeat to Columbus in MLS Cup playoffs.
Lionel Messi is at the centre of a controversy after hurling the ball at an opponent during a throw-in and after the Columbus Crew coach says the Inter Miami superstar should have been sent off instead of receiving a yellow card.
The incident took place on Saturday during Miami’s 3-0 home defeat by Columbus in the first game of a best-of-three series in the MLS Cup playoffs.
With 10-man Miami 1-0 down at the stroke of half-time, Messi’s frustration boiled over as he aimed a forceful throw-in into the face of Columbus Crew forward Gonzalo Tapia.
Tapia, less than a metre (3ft) away and trying to impede Messi’s actions, threw himself to the ground after the ball hit his face while Messi appealed for a handball.

“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said in a postgame news conference when asked about the incident.
According to the International Football Association Board Law 12 , which pertains to fouls and misconduct, the appropriate disciplinary action for such an incident would be both players being “cautioned (yellow card) for unsporting behaviour”.
It adds that the player taking the throw-in could be “sent off (red card) for violent conduct (if the thrower used excessive force)”.
Chapman defended his decision to brandish a yellow card to Messi.
“The force used was negligible, and the offence did not reach the level of violent conduct,” the referee told a pool reporter.
Tapia, who scored twice for Columbus in the win, refrained from commenting on the referee’s decision, saying, “I don’t know if it’s a red card, but I am not the referee to say. It stays there.”
Miami head coach Kily Gonzalez also echoed Tapia’s thoughts, adding that the “card doesn’t change much”.
“The referee saw a yellow, and that is it. We can’t blame the referee,” Gonzalez told reporters. “Sometimes they make mistakes. Sometimes they don’t like each one of us, and we have to accept it.”
The 3-0 defeat means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, could eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in game two of the series in Ohio on Friday.
“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Gonzalez said.
“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out,” he added.

Protests held on sixth weekend as tens of thousands march over inequality and organisers plan more rallies.
Tens of thousands of people have marched in cities across France for the sixth consecutive weekend to demand better public services and express anger over the rising cost of living and deepening inequality.
The protest movement, sparked in mid-September by high school students calling for improved learning conditions, has since fuelled a nationwide campaign against soaring prices, failing public services and police brutality.
Across the country, organisers reported 150,000 protesters on Saturday, down from 200,000 last week and 800,000 during the first of the weekly demonstrations on October 17.
The Ministry of the Interior said numbers have “significantly declined” as it put Saturday’s turnout at 82,500 people, compared with 106,000 a week earlier.
The protests have been largely peaceful but have seen sporadic violence on the margins and repeated accusations of police brutality.
Last month, huge rallies across France descended into the worst rioting seen in years with hundreds of shops looted and buildings attacked and set on fire.
Unions and activists have called for further protests in the coming weeks.

Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes
It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.
Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.
Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero .
Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.
It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play.
(WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.)
Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.)
Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.
Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb.
Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film.
The film ends on a suitably bittersweet note, and while Yamazaki hasn’t dropped any hints about a possible third film in the series, we’d love to learn more about Noriko’s strangely symbiotic connection to Godzilla via the G-cells in her bloodstream. Long may he reign.

The footage, recorded by a driver travelling through Lviv on Friday 20 November, shows the moment a projectile struck a building directly ahead of the vehicle . The impact sent debris across the road and forced the driver to reverse sharply before driving away.
Two people were killed and at least 10 others injured in Lviv’s Zaliznychnyi district as a large-scale Russian missile and drone barrage tore across the western Ukrainian city and its surrounding region, igniting fires in residential blocks and garages. According to Ukrainian authorities, the bombardment left a trail of destruction spanning homes, vehicles, a dormitory, a warehouse and critical energy infrastructure, while also damaging a ticket terminal at Sknyliv railway station .
The fallout extended beyond the city limits into the nearby Zolochiv district , where debris from a downed Russian drone damaged three houses and a vehicle, leaving one further person injured .
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles , including 27 ballistic missiles, in the wider assault. The strikes also affected Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine , underscoring the scale of the bombardment and the continuing threat to civilians and essential infrastructure.

ChatGPT ve benzeri yapay zeka uygulamaları öğrenciler arasında yaygınlaşıyor. Araştırmalar, yapay zekanın bilinçsiz kullanımının okul başarısını ve temel becerileri olumsuz etkileyebileceğini gösteriyor.
Yapay zeka uygulamaları öğrenciler arasında giderek yaygınlaşıyor. 15 yaşındaki 9'uncu sınıf öğrencisi Jakob, kendisinin ve arkadaşlarının yaklaşık iki buçuk yıldır yapay zekayı kullandığını anlatıyor. DW'ye konuşan ve gerçek adını söylemek istemeyen Jakob, "Bugün Fransızca sınavım vardı ve dün ChatGPT'den birçok konuyu yeniden açıklamasını istedim. Sınıfımdakilerin çoğu, ev ödevlerini yaptırmak için yapay zeka kullanıyor" diyor.
Matematik, Almanca, İngilizce, kimya veya fizik fark etmiyor, tek bir tıklama ile çözüm veya çözüm yolu ekrana geliyor. Bilim dünyasında bu "düşünme sürecinin başka araçlara aktarılması" olarak tanımlanıyor. Bu durumda düşünme eylemi başka bir araca devrediliyor, bu bir hesap makinesi, bir not kağıdı ya da ChatGPT gibi bir sohbet robotu olabiliyor.
Ancak beyin açısından sorun, problemin tamamının yapay zeka tarafından çözülmesiyle başlıyor. Bir not kağıdı veya hesap makinesi çözüm sürecindeki bazı adımları üstlense de genellikle tüm düşünme sürecini devralmaz. Yapay zeka sohbet robotları ise bunun çok ötesine geçiyor.
Bazen ev ödevlerini yapay zekaya yaptırdığını söyleyen Jakob, ancak "sadece gerçekten çıkmaza girdiği" durumlarda yapay zekaya başvurduğunu anlatıyor. Bunun bir sorun olabileceğinin farkında olan Jakob, "Notları iyi olanlar, bunu pek yapmıyor" diyor.
Yıllardır Almanca öğretmenliği yapan Franziska Müller, bir lisede çalışıyor. DW'ye konuşan Müller, bazı öğrencileri için "Artık kendi başlarına düşünemiyorlar" şeklindeki gözlemini aktarıyor. Adını değiştirdiğimiz Müller, bazı öğrencilerin derste soruları yapay zekaya yazdığını, sıra gelince de fark ettirmeden yapay zekanın verdiği yanıtları okuduklarını anlatıyor.
Öğrencilerin geçmişe kıyasla metinleri kavramakta daha çok zorlandığını söyleyen Müller, "Çünkü daha az okuyorlar ve neredeyse her şeyi yapay zekaya özetletiyorlar" diyor.
Eylül ayında açıklanan PISA araştırması gibi, birçok çalışma benzer sonuçları ortaya koyuyor. Ekonomik İşbirliği ve Kalkınma Örgütü'nün (OECD) yaptırdığı PISA araştırmasını yürütenler, "Belirli ödevlerde yapay zeka sohbet robotlarını kullanan öğrenciler, fen bilimlerinde yapay zekayı kullanmayan öğrencilere kıyasla daha düşük puanlar alıyor" sonucuna vardı.
90'dan fazla ülkeden öğrencilerin katıldığı araştırma, 15 yaş grubuna yönelik dünyanın en kapsamlı uluslararası karşılaştırma çalışması olarak kabul ediliyor. Almanya'daki öğrenciler bu yıl araştırmada şimdiye kadarki en kötü sonuçlardan birini aldı.
PISA'nın yapay zekaya ilişkin bulguları ise oldukça basit: "Nasıl yalnızca spor izleyerek değil, spor yaparak formda kalabiliyorsak; öğrenme de sadece içerik tüketerek değil, bilgi üzerinde düşünerek ve zihinsel çaba harcayarak gerçekleşiyor." Başka bir deyişle, beyinlerini yeterince çalıştırmayanlar, düşünme becerilerini köreltme riskiyle karşı karşıya kalabilir.
ABD merkezli düşünce kuruluşu Brookings Institution eğitim alanında yapay zekânın risklerinin faydalarından daha ağır bastığını savunuyor. Dünyanın farklı ülkelerinden gençlerin katıldığı araştırmada, "temel becerilerin kaybı" ile "eleştirel düşünme, hafıza, odaklanma ve muhakeme yeteneğinin zayıflaması" risklerine dikkat çekiliyor.
Peki, ChatGPT, Claude, Grok veya Meta AI gibi yapay zeka sohbet robotlarının eğitimde giderek artan etkisi karşısında ne yapılmalı?
New York'un sol görüşlü belediye başkanı Zohran Mamdani, 2026-2027 eğitim öğretim yılında devlet okullarında 8'inci sınıfa kadar, yani 14-15 yaşına dek yapay zeka kullanımını yasakladı.
Yasak bir çözüm olabilir mi? Almanya'da ortaöğretim veren bir okulda 10'uncu ve 13'üncü sınıflara Almanca dersi veren Julian Hinn yasağın çözüm olmadığı görüşünde. Herkesin cep telefonu üzerinden yapay zekaya erişebildiğini belirten Hinn, "Bunu evde kullanmayacaklarını düşünenler, gerçekleri görmezden geliyor" diyor.
Almanya'da gençlerin medya kullanımına ilişkin JIM araştırması da bu görüşü destekliyor. Almanya'da bu araştırmaya katılan 12-19 yaş arasındaki gençlerin yüzde 91'i en az bir yapay zeka uygulamasını kullandığını ifade etti. Yüzde 74'ü de yapay zekayı ev ödevlerini yaparken ve ders çalışırken kullandığını belirtti. Bu veriler 2024 yılına ait. Günümüzde bu oranın artmış olabileceği tahmin ediliyor. Brookings Institute'un Asya, Latin Amerika ve ABD'de yaptığı araştırma da gençler arasında yapay zeka kullanımının benzer seviyelerde olduğunu gösteriyor.
Alman siyasetçiler de sorunun farkında. Almanya'da eğitim eyalet yönetimlerinin yetki alanında yer almasına rağmen, Eğitim Bakanları Konferansı, 2024 yılından beri yapay zekanın kullanımına ilişkin tavsiyelerde bulunuyor. Bu tavsiye kararları yasaklama yerine öğrencilerin yapay zekaya eleştirel yaklaşması ve bu konuda becerilerinin geliştirilmesi gerektiğini içeriyor.
Öte yandan yapay zekanın eğitimde önemli bir destek sağlayabileceği de açık. "Yapay zeka konuları ders kitaplarından çok daha iyi anlatıyor" diyen Jakob, bu nedenle birçok temel konuyu yapay zekâdan yardım alarak öğrenmeyi tercih ettiğini söylüyor.
Öğretmen Julian Hinn de bu görüşe katılıyor: "Yapay zeka, öğrencilerin kullandığı dile ve ihtiyaçlarına çok daha iyi uyum sağlayabiliyor. Öğretmenlerin bunu her zaman yapması mümkün olmayabiliyor."
Hinn, bu nedenle de öğrencilerin 10'uncu sınıftan itibaren yapay zeka ile çalışmaya başlamasını önemli buluyor. Üst sınıflarda ise öğrencileri bilinçli olarak yapay zekaya soru sormaya teşvik ediyor. Hinn, "Daha sonra öğrencilerle birlikte verilen yanıtların kalitesini değerlendiriyoruz" diyor.
9'uncu sınıfa kadar ise yapay zekanın daha sınırlı bir şekilde kullanılması gerektiği görüşünde olan Hinn, bunun nedenini "Bu dönemde temel becerilerin henüz gelişme aşamasında olması" olarak açıklıyor.
Franziska Müller de üst sınıflarda yapay zeka uygulamalarını derslerinde daha sık kullanıyor. Ancak bazı aşamalarda öğrencilerin kendi başlarına düşünmelerini sağlamak amacıyla bu araçların kullanımını tamamen yasakladığı da oluyor. Müller, "Yapay zeka kullanmanın ne kadar cazip olduğunu çok iyi anlayabiliyorum" diyor.
Yapay zeka doğru kullanıldığında öğrencilerin başarısını artırabilirken, yanlış şekilde kullanıldığında ise öğrenme sürecini olumsuz etkileyebiliyor. Ancak araştırmaların ortaya koyduğu başka bir sorun daha var: Yapay zekâ, eğitimdeki eşitsizlikleri büyütebilir.
Brookings Institution'ın araştırmasına göre, temel becerileri sağlam olan öğrenciler yapay zeka sayesinde öğrenmelerini daha da geliştirebiliyor ve akranlarına kıyasla daha hızlı ilerleyebiliyor.
Buna karşılık temel bilgi eksiklikleri bulunan öğrenciler, yapay zekanın hatalı yanıtlarını daha kolay kabul ediyor, düşünme sürecini bu araçlara devredebiliyor ve sonuç olarak daha da geride kalabiliyor.
PISA araştırması da daha avantajlı sosyoekonomik koşullara sahip ailelerden gelen çocukların genellikle eğitime daha güçlü bir başlangıç yaptığını ortaya koyuyor. Bu durum, yapay zekanın eğitimdeki fırsat eşitsizliğini daha da artırabileceğine işaret ediyor. Başlangıçta avantajlı olanlar daha hızlı ilerlerken, dezavantajlı konumdakiler geride kalabiliyor.
Yapay zeka yaygınlaşırken öğretmenlere de önemli görevler düşüyor. Öğretmenlerin, öğrencileri düşünmeye teşvik etmeleri ve onlara kendi sorumluluklarını hatırlatmaları gerekiyor.
Okul gazetesi çıkardığını belirten Julian Hinn, "Öğrencilere her zaman şunu söylüyorum: Yapay zeka kullanabilirsiniz, ancak sonunda kendi kaleminizden çıkmış bir yazı yazmış olmanın verdiği duygu bambaşka" diyor.
Hinn de Müller de öğrencilerin bireysel sorumluluğun önemini kavrayabileceği konusunda iyimser. Çünkü aksi durumda bunun sonuçları en geç yazılı sınavlarda ortaya çıkıyor. Bu sınavlarda herhangi bir yardımcı araç kullanılmıyor.
Böylece öğrenciler, konuları gerçekten kendi başlarına anlayıp anlayamadıklarıyla yüzleşmek zorunda kalıyor.
Franziska Müller'in anlattığı bir örnek de bunu gös…

A new COP31 draft agreement was published early on Sunday as nations continued to struggle to reach a climate deal.
The new draft, published deep into overtime, kept a much-sought goal to electrify the global economy but again failed to mention fossil fuels, deepening divisions at the UN conference - which is being held in Antalya, Turkey.
The latest text needs consensus approval from almost 200 nations at a closing session on Sunday.
An EU official told the AFP news agency that the draft was a "backwards" step and warned that there was a "very real possibility" of the talks ending without a deal.
"I am more pessimistic today than I was yesterday," they said.
"The situation is difficult, and the outcome is uncertain. The oil-producing countries are putting up a fierce fight," a German official added.
Planet-heating fossil fuels have become a flashpoint at the talks, which come amid soaring energy prices and simmering global tensions stemming from the Iran war.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week had called for a sped-up phasing out of fossil fuels. But a second version released on Thursday removed all mentions of the energy sources, forcing negotiators back to the bargaining table.
A group of countries including France and Panama had released a letter on Friday insisting that a deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."
The latest offering acknowledged a previous global deal to transition away from fossil fuels but stopped short of naming them explicitly.
It also kept a contentious push to expand carbon capture and storage, a technology backed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised by opponents as costly and ineffective at reducing emissions.
"We are very disappointed with how the text looks," Michael Joseph, the environment minister of Antigua and Barbuda, told AFP.
"I can't honestly say that I'm okay with it passing" as it is, Joseph said, adding that the draft was "quite silent" on fossil fuels.

New draft would acknowledge for the first time that global ⁠warming is on course to pass 1.5C.
The fate of United Nations climate talks in Turkiye is hanging in the balance as the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) co-presidents, Australia and Turkiye, struggle to secure consensus on a deal to advance the fight against climate change, raising ⁠⁠the prospect of no deal being reached.
The new draft of the deal was released on Sunday, two days after the conference in Antalya was scheduled to end.
If approved, it would acknowledge for the first time that global ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.
The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the centre of frictions at the talks. Instead, it includes language referring to ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌a previous COP at which governments had agreed to transition away from oil, gas and coal.
“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a plenary session early on Sunday.
Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, said the conference would reconvene later on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
Other delegations at the venue, where catering outlets and exhibits have already been dismantled, were less sure.
French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said the proposal was a “backward” step. “Time is ticking and we are not there yet,” she said.
An earlier draft had provoked strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels, the largest contributors to climate change.
Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the continued omission in the new draft, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.
“Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era and our leaders are on ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the verge of falling for it,” said Sara Shaw, the group’s campaigns and networks ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.
Observers at the closed-door talks said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing nations had pushed hard to keep fossil fuels out of the ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠text and carbon removal in.
A representative of the Saudi delegation declined to comment.
Kurum said he ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠believed concerns around fossil fuels had ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌been addressed, as had those ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌around helping developing countries finance their adaptation to climate change.
The new ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌leading the talks; Turkiye, which is hosting the meeting; and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.
The summit’s agreement is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heatwaves, floods and other disasters.
An opening draft from Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.
Key issues that slowed the agreement included how much effort countries should make to wean themselves off fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas.
Other issues included whether to encourage industrial carbon capture and storage of pollutants, as well as whether ramping up electricity generation should only be done with renewables, such as wind and solar, or also involve other sources such as natural gas and coal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions.
The two-week talks in the Turkish city were due to end on Friday.
In a letter sent on Saturday to this year’s cohosts, Turkiye and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the UN has ever held.
The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations”.
In the lead-up to these talks, the UN said the world would likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial temperatures.

Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.
Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.
The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.
"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media. , external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.
Riding a wave of momentum created by a 54th-minute Olimpico from midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo, and capping it off with an all-important breakaway winner from Debinha, the Current silenced the partisan, sellout crowd at the heavily-favored Washington Spirit’s home ground with a 2-1 victory on Saturday.
The Spirit, heartbroken at the final whistle, have now lost three consecutive NWSL Championships.
“Obviously this one hates way worse than any of the other ones,” forward Trinity Rodman said afterward. “I don’t even think you have words in this moment — it is too fresh.”
DiBernardo’s goal was stunning, a driven, bent corner kick played to the far post that eluded Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver, her defenders and Current forward Haley Hopkins, potentially DiBernardo’s intended target. The Spirit’s players and fans alike pleaded with center referee Joshua Encarnación, suggesting he examine the play on VAR for obstruction, as MacIver had potentially been screened. The review never came.
Whether played directly on goal intentionally or otherwise, the effort will go down as one of the most memorable in NWSL Championship history. At 34, DiBernardo becomes the oldest player in league history to score in a final, and was later named the match’s MVP.
“I’ve been to the game a few times and haven’t won, but this one just felt a little lighter,” said DiBernardo, who gave birth to Charlie, her first child, in January and took time off before returning to the Current in March. “I think just having Charlie, it just brings a different perspective on life. I knew the game was big and it was a big moment, but just kinda having her, just spending the day with her, it just felt really special.”
The game’s early phases were forgettable save for one incident which would go on to affect the remainder of the match: a bruising, high-speed tackle on Rodman by Current defender Laney Rouse in the fifth minute. The challenge sent Rodman flying and appeared to injure her left elbow; the Spirit forward, nearing tears, spent much of the first half in visible pain and seemingly never fully recovered. Rouse was not cautioned for the challenge.
“[It helped set the tone] in the sense that it hurt really bad, yes,” Rodman said. “As a team, you always want to put the first hit in. You’re taught to do that. Credit to them. I wish I was the one who put her on the ground. They did a really good job at setting the tone and controlling the first half.”
It was far from the game’s only physical moment. Neither team managed to settle into any meaningful rhythm during an opening 45 that felt at times more like a title fight than a title match. Encarnación, involved in his first NWSL final, called a very tight match and the near-constant stoppages in play were the defining characteristic of a sometimes ugly opening phase. In many ways it was not entirely his fault: the message-sending start from KC and the Spirit’s subsequent response often compelled him to act. The 19 combined first-half fouls between both sides were the most in any half of any NWSL title match in league history.
“It felt like we couldn’t play more than two minutes without a whistle,” Rodman said. “We were fouling, they were true calls for sure — but I think you lose control of the game really quickly that way ... It definitely messed with our rhythm a little bit.”
Paradoxically, though, the match was won with speed. Deep into second-half stoppage time, the Current found their eventual match-winner on a breakaway. After doggedly winning back possession after a Spirit free kick late on, Kansas City forward Debinha streaked upfield from just beyond the center stripe, looking off a wide-open Temwa Chawinga and rounding MacIver who looked on hopelessly as the Brazilian slotted it home.
Moments later, Rodman – somehow still in the match after not only the early challenge but a later high-speed collision with Current goalkeeper Lorena – pulled one back for the Spirit. Falling away from goal 10 yards out, Rodman got her head on the end of a Tara Rudd cross, placing it perfectly over Lorena’s outstretched arms and into the far-side netting. The ensuing five minutes – the game ended in the 102nd – were chaotic but the Spirit couldn’t quite find the equalizer.
After a slow start, the Current were well-managed by former Major League Soccer and US national team member Chris Armas. Armas was widely considered a controversial selection at the time of his appointment but proceeded to lead the club to their first championship in his first season, doing so by beating Gotham FC and now the Spirit, two sides picked by many as potential league-winners.
“I think from the front to the back we made it a point that every person on this team defends and if somebody is going to make a mistake the other person is going to have their back,” Current defender Izzy Rodriguez said. “We try and turn every 1v1 situation into a 1v2 for us, and I think that showed up today. We were winning our duels and second balls and those are things that win games.”
For the Spirit, the loss is devastating. They become the first American professional club – men’s or women’s – to lose three consecutive finals since the New England Revolution of Major League Soccer, who did so in the mid 2000s. In their five Championship appearances, the Spirit have won just one time, in 2021.

Cumhurbaşkanlığı İletişim Başkanlığı, Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın NATO, BM, Türk Devletleri Teşkilatı ve COP31 zirvelerindeki yoğun diplomasi trafiğini, liderlerle gerçekleştirdiği kritik görüşmeleri ve zirvelerden çok özel anları içeren "Türkiye'nin Diplomasi Rotası: Dört Zirvede Lider Diplomasisi" belgeselini hazırladı.
Cumhurbaşkanlığı İletişim Başkanı Burhanettin Duran, NSosyal hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda, küresel dengelerin yeniden şekillendiği, savaşların ve krizlerin dünya gündemini belirlediği bir dönemde Türkiye'nin Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın liderliğinde diplomasi alanındaki etkinliğini her geçen gün artırdığını belirtti.

Former PM who opted for minimal ties with bloc says moves towards membership would dominate government’s time
Theresa May has said she feels “aghast” at Andy Burnham’s plan for potentially rejoining the EU, arguing in a rare interview that the prime minister should “accept Brexit and move on”.
Speaking to the BBC after Friday’s UK-EU summit , at which Burnham secured the biggest step towards renewed ties with Brussels since Brexit, May said that a further move towards membership, as talked about by the PM, would dominate the government’s time.
“What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that had to be put in,” said May, who took over in No 10 from David Cameron shortly after the 2016 referendum and shaped the basics of the very hard departure deal that Boris Johnson eventually sealed.
“It’s across the whole of government. It’s not just prime ministerial time, [it’s] cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations, because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want.
“That’s one of the reasons why I looked slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham was talking about – further negotiations of going into the EU. As a country, we voted for Brexit .
“When I was prime minister, I was very clear: we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is: people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.”
May said it was damaging for governments not to trust the results of referendums: “I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people … He wants to pat them on the head and say: ‘You know what? Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer’ – what he thinks is the right answer.”
May’s intervention is an unusual step from the former prime minister, who has typically reserved her public statements since leaving office for areas of cross-party consensus. On taking office, she opted to push for minimal residual ties with the EU as a way to maintain unity in the Conservatives. But she struggled with the Brussels negotiations amid dissent among her MPs, and was ousted in 2019 .
Pressed on whether Brexit had been a success, May refused to say, arguing that with global shocks such as Covid and Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine, it was impossible to know.
Asked outright if she believed the UK was in a better or worse state as a result of the decision to leave the EU, she replied: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union .”
The summit in Brussels on Friday saw the announcement of three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.
Burnham, who has condemned the May-Johnson departure deal for hampering growth and gumming up trade, has raised the possibility of even closer ties and that the UK could rejoin the EU in the future.
None of this would happen until after another election, with Burnham committed until then to the Brexit “red lines” of Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which rules out being part of the EU’s customs union or single market.
While the changes in the new deal will be presented to parliament as a bill next week, at the summit, Burnham slightly slowed down the pace of any further moves. He said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, with the timetable talked about in terms of months, while reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.
The Conservatives have been pushing back against the deal made on Friday, briefing newspapers on Sunday that signing up to the emissions trading system would add costs to domestic energy bills because of EU carbon taxes.
Downing Street argues the deal will bring down energy and food costs, with Burnham saying on Friday it could add as much as 0.5% to GDP in the long term.

Foreign secretary says there is clear case to integrate more closely but does not say if he backs talks on possibly rejoining
Closer links with the EU will mean the UK having a say on decisions made by Brussels, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has argued as ministers faced pressure to move further after Friday’s landmark deal with the EU.
Any timetable for closer integration, including possible talks about the UK rejoining the EU, remains unclear after the Brussels summit, with Andy Burnham saying he would now “brainstorm” over future ties.
Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, said Burnham should now push for membership.
“The problem with being outside the bloc is that we end up in a permanent state of negotiation, because we always have to play catchup, rather than having a seat at the table,” she wrote in an article for the Sunday Mirror. “That’s why I think we should simply be back in the European Union.”
Speaking to BBC One’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show, Miliband refused to say whether he now supported discussions on potentially rejoining, but said the deal reached at Friday’s summit – on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual youth mobility scheme – showed the benefits of closer links, including UK input to EU regulations that were being followed anyway.
“At the moment, what the situation is is that we are essentially rule takers,” he said. “Businesses are rule takers if they want to sell into the European market. So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union , but at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms.”
He said this was “the worst of all worlds” and it meant there was a clear case to integrate more closely into EU markets.
Another reason for even closer ties, he said, was the transformed geopolitical order since 2016, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the US’s distancing from Europe under Donald Trump.
He said: “I was not in favour of Brexit , as you know, but I accepted the result, and I think it was right to accept the result. [But] I think there’s a key point: the world has changed massively since 2016, and we can’t stand still.
“How can we say ‘well, this is all it is, the status quo is fine, even with the summit today. We’re not even going to look at the future of our relationship with the European Union.’ Of course, we’ve got to do that, and we’ve got to lay out the options.”
Speaking for the Conservatives on the Sunday morning broadcast round, Alex Burghart, Kemi Badenoch’s deputy, said Burnham should simply be concentrating on better defence ties with Europe, arguing that the public would not want to return to the EU.
Asked if the Conservatives would undo the deal made at Friday’s summit if they won power, Burghart said they would. He said: “Yes, we would scrap it. I don’t think that there will be good outcomes from it. And I also don’t think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future. This is a silly idea.”
Burnham faces some nervousness in his cabinet and the parliamentary Labour party more widely over talk of possibly rejoining, with some MPs wary about the bitter political fight this could set off.
But Thornberry in her article praised Burnham for having “finally ended the conspiracy of silence over Brexit”, saying polls indicated that a majority of the UK public now backed rejoining.

Trinity Rodman left in tears after scoring Spirit’s only goal as DiBernardo and Debinha give Current closely-fought win.
Kansas City Current have defeated the Washington Spirit in a closely-contested final to be crowned the NWSL champions for the first time as Trinity Rodman’s bid to avoid a third consecutive final defeat ended in bitter disappointment in Washington, DC.
Vanessa DiBernardo curled in a goal direct from a corner and Brazilian international Debinha added a second in stoppage time to set up Kansas City’s 2-1 victory at Audi Field on Saturday.
Rodman headed in a 98th-minute goal to pull one back for Spirit, but Kansas City held on to win.
“We knew it was going to be a battle; we felt good coming out of the first half,” said DiBernardo, who was named the championship MVP months after returning to professional football following the birth of her daughter.
It was another crushing loss for United States star Rodman and her Spirit teammates, who were also beaten in the final in 2025 and 2024.
Rodman, who was in tears at the final whistle, was knocked out of her stride earlier in the game.
The 24-year-old was on the receiving end of a rugged aerial challenge from Kansas City’s Laney Rouse after just five minutes and needed treatment on the sidelines.
Rodman returned to the field grimacing in pain and clutching her shoulder but completed the game.
The opening goal came early in the second half, with DiBernardo’s in-swinging corner looping into the net after Kansas City’s Kayla Sharples cleverly blocked Washington goalkeeper Sandy MacIver.
Deep in stoppage time, Debinha added Current’s second after a sweeping counterattack, before Rodman’s header was too little, too late.
The victory was Kansas City’s first NWSL title after losing in the championship game to the Portland Thorns in 2022.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said at least 14 people were missing after a Russian drone struck a five-story residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, injuring two others. Meanwhile, Finland warned the war was "spilling over" after a drone set fire to a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
Schools in Odesa will switch to remote teaching after Russian strikes gravely damaged the energy grid in the major Ukrainian Black Sea port city, the authorities said on Sunday.
Russia has carried out a wide-ranging campaign of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure, with the prospect of another freezing wartime winter looming.
Citing "serious interruptions in heat, electricity and water supply", Odesa's municipal education department decreed a period of home-learning from November 23 to 27.
It advised residents to "charge phones, tablets and laptops as soon as possible so that children can use them to study".
Ukrenergo, the country's energy supplier, warned on Sunday that the electricity situation in and around the city "remains extremely difficult".
"The consequences of the Russian attacks are massive," the company said on social media.
"Russia launched around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs, and 165 missiles of various types at them," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X.
"A significant number were ballistic missiles, including North Korean ones, which the Russians are constantly helping Pyongyang modernize to improve their accuracy," he continued.
Zelensky urged the US to approve the transfer of Patriot air defence missiles already paid for by Kyiv's partners, saying delays were "difficult to understand".
He also called on allies to continue contributing to the PURL programme, which he described as Ukraine's main source of anti-ballistic interceptors.
Ukraine's restaurant sector employs about 150,000 people and generated about 248 billion hryvnias ($5 billion) in sales last year, according to the National Restaurant Association.
Visitors enjoy their food while chef Anton cooks a meal in a wood-fired oven at a Chornomorka seafood restaurant in Kyiv, Ukraine, on November 14, 2026. © Valentyn Ogirenko, Reuters
During the war, restaurant owners have had to adapt to the difficult circumstances. Generators hum outside kitchens during long blackouts and many restaurants have installed large water tanks to cope with cuts to mains supply. Some have even bought their own water trucks to prepare for long-term disruptions.
Chornomorka, a sea food chain, has developed an "emergency menu" which can be served without running water and electricity, its development director Dmytro Kostrubin said, while some restaurants were prepared to cook some dishes outdoors over an open fire.
But it's getting more difficult to stay in business, especially as annual inflation hit 11% in October and some owners have already exhausted their financial reserves.
"The restaurant business is now in a very difficult situation," said Dmytro Pohrebitskyi, co-owner of the Pesto Cafe chain. "In five years of the war, from my experience, this is the most complicated period in the restaurant business."

Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.
To address the shortage, the industry is investing in training. A vocational college in Kyiv opened a European Union-funded facility in March, where 26 10th graders have started a three-year program to become window, door and facade installers.
Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, explains to students window construction at a technical college in Kyiv, Ukraine, on November 4, 2026. © Evgeniy Maloletka, Reuters

Brexit – or reversing it, 10 years after the event – is the topic dominating the Sunday politics shows this morning after major deals were struck with the EU on Friday on trade, travel, emissions and visas for young people.
Andy Burnham says these are the first steps towards rebuilding “the bridges broken all of those years ago” with “our nearest neighbours and our largest market”.
While he’s voiced support for re-joining the bloc, he’s also stressed that all options are on the table and there’s a long road ahead in convincing the British public and securing the unanimous assent needed from the 27-nation bloc.
Critics have piled in this morning, warning how tricky of an endeavour this could be. Ex-PM Theresa May , whose government was brought down by Brexit in 2019, has told the BBC that the divorce “is done” and he should “move on”.
That interview’s coming up on Laura Kuenssberg’s show later this morning. Meanwhile over on Sky, Brexiteer Michael Gove is hosting Reform and Tory naysayers as well as the European relations minister. I’ll recap their comments.

double quotation mark One area where the UK is absolutely and completely united across the whole political spectrum is standing with Ukraine against Russia’s barbaric, illegal war.
So would Vladimir Putin be my friend? No. And he’s not a friend of the UK either.”

double quotation mark The Prime Minister speaks to the president regularly, and is in absolutely no way pulling his punches about the strength of feeling that the UK has as a whole about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Çift şubatta da ortak fotoğraflarını silmiş, ancak kısa süre sonra ayrılık iddialarını boşa çıkarmıştı. İki isimden henüz açıklama gelmedi.

TRT 1'de 2023 'te yayınlanan dizide Alize ile Serkan'ı canlandıran ikilinin set arkadaşlığı kısa sürede aşka dönüşmüştü. Çift ilişkisini hiç saklamadı; tatilleri, konserleri ve özel günleri sosyal medyada sık sık gündem oldu.
İkili bugün Instagram 'da birbirini takipten çıktı. Hamle kısa sürede dikkat çekti. Üstelik zamanlama da manidar. Enes Koçak, daha bir ay önce Eylül Tumbar'la ilişkisi sorulduğunda 'Hayatımın şükür dönemindeyim' demişti.
Peki ünlü çift yollarını ayırdı mı? Şimdilik ne Koçak'tan ne de Tumbar'dan bir açıklama var.

18 Eylül'de konuşan Eylül Tumbar da ilişkilerinin sürdüğünü doğrulamış, 'Enes sette, çalışıyor' demişti. Evlilik sorusuna ise 'Evlilik gibi bir planımız yok' yanıtını vermişti.

Güney Amerika Futbol Konfederasyonu tarafından düzenlenen kıtanın kulüp düzeyindeki en önemli ikinci turnuvası olan Sudamericana Kupası finalinde Boca Juniors ile Atletico Mineiro kozlarını paylaştı.
Kolombiya'nın Barranquilla kentindeki Metropolitano Roberto Melendez Stadı'nda oynanan karşılaşmayı 16. dakikada Santiago Ascacibar ve 48. dakikada Miguel Merentiel'in attığı gollerle 2-0 kazanan Boca Juniors, 2004 ve 2005'in ardından üçüncü kez şampiyonluğa ulaştı.
